📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, declared the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.

In a recent development, in the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

See all results for used Toyota for sale near 95123.

The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.

Recent findings suggest that the push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into latest innovations.

Recent findings suggest that “We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato mentioned. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”.

Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI.
  • Also: I checked Gemini’s newly introduced Memory summary to see what it knew about me.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback.

Also: I checked Gemini’s newly introduced Memory summary to see what it knew about me.

Recent findings suggest that in a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road.

Industry observers note that right now, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two.

To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two newly introduced settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes.

“With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google stated in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.

Industry observers note that here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats.

Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history.

It has been revealed that chatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.”.

Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027.

It has been revealed that in all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the firm take this step in the right direction.

#62435. 11 Steps I Use for Quick Smart Home Prep for Guests and Holiday Visitors

11 Steps I Use for Quick Smart Home Prep for Guests and Holiday Visitors

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as smart home and home security devices become more common, we’ve all got more devices around our homes when guests come over.
  • If you have holiday or event plans involving guests, especially guests staying over a day or two, I highly suggest making these adjustments to your smart home devices.
  • Read more: The 7 Most Common Home Security Mistakes to Stop Making.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as smart home and home security devices become more common, we’ve all got more devices around our homes when guests come over. Since I test home security and multiple smart devices, I tend to have a lot. But they don’t have to be a distraction when you have visitors staying over. On the contrary, smart tech can usually help out.

If you have holiday or event plans involving guests, especially guests staying over a day or two, I highly suggest making these adjustments to your smart home devices. These changes save me headaches and time, while impressing guests. You may even decide to enable some features year-round.

Read more: The 7 Most Common Home Security Mistakes to Stop Making.

Doorbell chimes are just the start of your smart guest experience.

It has been revealed that video doorbells often come with a feature in settings to switch to seasonal themes, including a variety of holiday sounds for the end of the year. Vivint is particularly good at this, equipping its video doorbell with options for many different holiday songs. Google Nest doorbells and Eufy doorbells also have holiday options.

Smart lighting is easy to set up for certain times of day, dimming and brightening as necessary.

In a recent development, cameras and guests don’t play well together. Help everyone feel safe by pulling down the shutters on your indoor cameras, nanny cams and smart displays (or disabling them through settings, etc.). Let everyone know their privacy is secured while staying over. Video doorbells and outdoor cams are fine to leave functioning, especially if you want to keep an eye on kids going crazy in your backyard.

Today’s smart lights include options to turn on at certain times of day or at sunrise, and at a specific brightness (and even color temperature). Some even allow you to gradually increase the brightness over an hour or so. Use these settings to set a simulated sunrise in key spots of the house to encourage guests to rise and shine at the right times. It’s especially handy if everyone needs to be up in the morning for a special activity — but make sure to provide coffee too.

Aqara’s app distills a whole lot of smart lock options into a highly digestible product card.

Industry observers note that A smart lock allows for all kinds of tricks, like remote operation and auto-locking if it’s left unlocked. Those work great when you have guests over, but if you want to add even more options, many locks allow you to create temporary passes — including through common apps like Apple Home — and send them to your guest’s phones. That way they can come and go on their own schedules, and the door stays locked when no one is using it.

Today’s smart thermostats, including the Google Nest, have humidity sensors, too.

Industry observers note that keeping the thermostat triggering temperatures a bit low in winter is a great way to save energy, but not always the sign of a good host. Consider heading into your thermostat app and bumping up temperatures a few degrees, especially at night and the middle of the day, so everyone stays comfortable. The latest models can even sense humidity, which can be notable if guests are sensitive to very dry or very wet air.

ADT’s new hub has a few extra tricks.

Recent findings suggest that home security system schedules usually call for arming the system during the day after everyone has left the house. That doesn’t work so well over the holidays, especially if you have guests over. Instead of disabling individual sensors, we suggest setting your home security system to disarm during the day.

You can still get key alerts from devices like leak detectors or package-recognizing video doorbells with the system disarmed. And you can leave the night mode armed (which usually lets people move around but monitors doors and windows closely).

A guest Wi-Fi network is an excellent add-on if you have multiple people coming to visit. It lets you set a separate network and easy-to-remember password for all guest devices, keeping your home network safer and letting you prioritize key home devices. Plus, you can keep reusing it whenever people come over in the future. We’ve got a full guide on how to set a guest network up, but it’s usually very easy with app settings.

Prep your smart speakers for guests to avoid any problems.

Industry observers note that smart home speakers like an Echo or the fresh Apple HomeView are excellent devices for playing holiday music for a whole house. But there’s a small problem: With a lot of extra guest devices on your Wi-Fi, music streaming may not be reliable. You can solve this problem by downloading a playlist to a device like a phone or tablet and playing it on the smart speaker via Bluetooth. Many common apps like Spotify let you do this, especially if you have a subscription.

Sources indicate that voice assistants are handy and fun, but they can be a distraction when others are around, especially if kids start getting creative in their commands. You could turn voice assistants off entirely, but we like the option to limit what they can do.

For example, Alexa has a Voice ID section in its settings that allows you to limit skills and third-party services from working with any voice except the profiles you create and add for you and direct family members. Google Assistant has a very similar option with its Voice Match settings, which limits device controls to only certain voices.

It’s also a good idea to set up a voice code to confirm any purchases made over voice assistants, so people can’t buy something with just a command.

A wireless charger nearly anyone can use.

It has been revealed that with the ubiquitous Qi charging standard, wireless chargers can work with nearly any phone. Make things easier for your guests by setting out a wireless charger or two for them to use without managing a tangle of power adapters. Bonus points if you offer chargers that have multiple charging pads, sparing your outlets even more.

According to recent reports, if you have a little extra time, most home security systems can connect to compatible smart lighting and let you create routines to make them more useful. Specifically, we’ve had great results creating night mode routines for security sensors that turn on nearby smart bulbs at low brightness settings when motion is detected.

This way, if someone gets up in the middle of the night, they can have a soft light to help them find their way without disturbing anyone else.

Don’t have a home security system? You don’t need one: Devices like this $50 Philips Hue motion sensor work independently and can automatically tell smart lights what to do when someone approaches.

For more on protecting and utilizing your smart home, take a look at our favorite DIY home security systems, our list of the best smart home devices and our total smart home cheat sheet for all platforms.

If Your Social Security Benefit Is Above This Average, You're Ahead of Most Retirees

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:00AM EST.
  • According to recent reports, where does your monthly benefit check sit compared to the rest of the country?
  • Recent findings suggest that averages depend heavily on who you are and when you claimed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:00AM EST.

According to recent reports, where does your monthly benefit check sit compared to the rest of the country? As of October 2026, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA), the average monthly benefit for retired workers is $2,092.17. That amounts to about $25,106.04 per year. This single figure covers everyone from those who just claimed at 62 to retirees well into their 90s.

Recent findings suggest that averages depend heavily on who you are and when you claimed. For instance, the average for people aged 62 is $1,424.40 per month, while those aged 70 receive an average of $2,274.68. Gender also creates a significant gap in the final numbers.

It has been revealed that averages also vary between men and women across the entire retired-worker population. As of December 2025, according to the SSA, these were the monthly averages for men and women across all age groups. They reflect the combined impact of different career earnings and claiming choices.

Sources indicate that landing above the $2,092.17 benchmark isn't a matter of luck. The SSA calculates your benefit based on an average of your monthly wages across your 35 highest-earning years. It adjusts earlier wages for inflation and runs them through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. Higher lifetime earnings generally result in a larger monthly check.

Claiming age is the other primary lever for beating the average. Full retirement age (FRA) ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year, and it's 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. Claiming at age 62 can reduce your check by up to 30%, while waiting until 70 earns delayed retirement credits worth 8% per year.

It has been revealed that while beating the average is helpful, it's rarely enough to cover a full retirement. Social Security is designed to replace only about 40% of your pre-retirement income. However, the average senior household headed by someone 65 or older spends $61,432 per year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). That's much higher than the $25,106.04 annual average benefit.

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027 to help checks keep pace with inflation. That adjustment adds about $75 per month to the $2,092.17 average. Even with these raises, most retirees rely on savings or other income sources to bridge the gap between their benefits and their total living costs. Beating the Social Security average is not the goal; covering your actual retirement expenses is.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to increase your odds of claiming an above-average benefit, there are three things you must do. First, work at least 35 years before you apply for Social Security. This will ensure you have no zero-income years included in your benefit calculation, which would weigh down your checks.

In a recent development, second, do what you can to increase your income today. The larger your average income throughout your career, the larger your future Social Security checks will be.

Sources indicate that third, choose your claiming age carefully. Claiming Social Security early could make sense if you have a short life expectancy or don't have much in personal savings. Otherwise, you may get a larger lifetime benefit by delaying Social Security until your FRA or possibly until you qualify for your largest checks at age 70.

Here are the five new Chrome features on Googlebook OS to know about.

It has been revealed that if you’ve ever had to share your screen on a video call, you know how irritating it can be to switch tabs without having to repeatedly start and stop sharing. Also: 6 Chrome default settings I changed to instantly.

Recent findings suggest that when you hover over a collapsed vertical tab rail with your mouse or trackpad, it will expand, so you can read full tab titles, switch tabs, or manage groups. The rail will collapse again when you move the cursor away.

Recent findings suggest that the Chrome upgrade allows you to manually resize your vertical tab bar to view longer page titles when needed. The browser will remember your custom tab width, even after you open a new window or restart the browser. (You’ll just need to turn “Auto expand tabs on hover” off for it to work.).

You can now save individual Chrome Settings subpages as direct web addresses that you can type, bookmark, or link to directly (for example, chrome://settings/privacy), meaning you won’t have to go digging around in menus to change your preferences anymore. You can navigate between these Settings subpages with the Back and Forward buttons.

Industry observers note that the system’s “Save As” file picker is now enabled by default for menu save actions, such as “Save link as” and “Save image as,” so you can more easily rename files and select a destination folder. This includes Google Drive or external storage.

It has been revealed that also: Google Chrome running slow? 5 easy ways to speed it up fast.

Outside of these newly introduced features, a few of Chrome M157’s performance fixes include the ability to press Ctrl+L to reveal and select web addresses; keeping your bookmarks bar visible in fullscreen mode and while screen sharing; better media controls while using Picture-in-Picture mode; and the ability to partially translate PDFs within your browser.

If you have Chrome set up to automatically download and install updates, you won’t have to lift a finger to take advantage of the fresh features and performance boosts.

But if you’ve disabled automatic updates, you can manually revision by selecting the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of your Chrome window and navigating to Help > About Google Chrome > Relaunch.

Breaking: Perplexity and Intelligence

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities.
  • I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI.
  • Sources indicate that A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI.

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a latest window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1.

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

Sources indicate that A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

In a recent development, the primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post demonstrates how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

Recent findings suggest that the range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the latest perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

In a recent development, as AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change swiftly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

It has been revealed that given that the main way upcoming surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in at the moment dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:.

Recent findings suggest that difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.

In a recent development, not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

It’s key to note that “compressor” in this sense is something that is capable of performing compression by predicting unseen data, not a compressed artifact like a GZIP file - that is, the best compressor trained on a given corpus does not necessarily “remember” the contents of the corpus.

In practice, we generally track the log of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss.

The primary held-out datasets we’ve been using since GPT-3.5 are sourced from our internal codebase, and those are the numbers reported here (for a fixed snapshot).

Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.

Recent findings suggest that on the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI⁠.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini.
  • To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that says “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.).

A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get users familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other users. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s latest Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours.

When a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and revision in real time, Google says. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the upcoming feature more comparable.

Breaking: Polaroid’s Portable Printer Got Me Right Back Into Journaling

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I loved journaling as a child.
  • Sources indicate that I made multiple attempts to return to journaling throughout the years, with varying success.
  • Recently, however, I found a way for me to actually stick to the habit: a $110 Polaroid Hi-Print pocket printer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I loved journaling as a child. It helped me survive hormonal changes, the usual teen dramas, plus a hefty dose of existential angst. Then college called, and I moved to a different country, leaving behind my childhood, my Nirvana cassettes (I’m old, OK?) and, sadly, my journaling habit.

Sources indicate that I made multiple attempts to return to journaling throughout the years, with varying success. I’ve delved into bullet journals under the pretense of improving my productivity, but I gave up when it became too much effort. I’ve invested in multiple notebooks and planners, only to eventually neglect them.

Recently, however, I found a way for me to actually stick to the habit: a $110 Polaroid Hi-Print pocket printer.

It all began when I discovered the wondrous world of journaling TikTok. In short-form videos, creators would show off beautiful journal pages decorated with colored markers, stickers, washi tape and, yes, photos — specifically photos from portable printers because the prints are small enough to fit within the confines of a typical journal or planner. I really liked the idea of decking out my journal pages with photos of my everyday life. I knew I had to get one.

According to recent reports, after a bit of research, I decided on a couple of criteria. First, I wanted the printer to be a dye sublimation printer rather than a ZINK (Zero Ink) printer. Dye sublimation printers essentially use heat to transfer dye onto the paper, while ZINK printers use a special paper that activates under heat with no ink required (hence the name). Dye sublimation prints tend to be higher quality because it transfers the dye in layers of cyan, magenta and yellow, followed by a protective coating.

Second, I wanted the photo to be on sticky paper so that I didn’t have to mess around with glue to add these photos to my journal.

In a recent development, I found quite a number of dye sublimation pocket printers on the market, but the one that caught my eye immediately was the Polaroid Hi-Print 2×3 Generation 2 pocket printer. I fell in love with it the moment I saw it. The sleek white design, the Polaroid logo and that curved rainbow accent on the edge really sealed the deal for me. Call me a sucker for style, I guess.

Recent findings suggest that I purchased a Hi-Print 2×3 “starter set,” which includes the printer along with two 2×3 paper cartridges. Each cartridge has 10 photo sheets, and each sheet is made out of sticky back photo paper, which is exactly what I wanted. Both the Gen 2 and the prior Gen 1 are easy to find; the main difference is the newer one uses a USB-C charging port while the original uses the older Micro-USB port.

Sources indicate that getting started with the printer is simple enough: Download the Polaroid Hi-Print app, pair the printer with your phone and you’re ready to go. The app is fairly easy to navigate. I like that it lets you arrange your photos in collages so you’re not limited to just one photo per sheet. You can also decorate your prints with colorful frames or decorations. The printer even offers a mosaic option that lets you print out one substantial image using multiple sheets.

Since it’s a dye sublimation printer, the Hi-Print prints out photos in stages. It lays down the different colors in multiple passes (yellow in the first pass, magenta in the second pass, and so forth). Because of that, printing does take a while: around 60 seconds per photo.

But I don’t mind the delay, as the resulting photo quality is superb. The colors are vibrant and the overall image is nice and sharp. The contrast could be a little better, but for a little pocket printer, the quality definitely exceeded my expectations.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few downsides, however. The obvious one is that photo cartridges can be pretty expensive. One pack of 20 sheets is around $17, though you can get it for $14 each if you buy the 5-pack. That’s still almost 70 cents per 2×3 print. If you use multiple prints, that can add up pretty quickly.

Another downside is that it doesn’t have a super long battery life. It only has a 620mAh battery, which Polaroid claims will last up to 20 photo printing sessions. I only ever use this printer at home, so this isn’t a major deal for me, but I can see this being a potential disappointment if you want to bring this printer on the road. That stated, if you do want to charge it, it doesn’t take that long. Polaroid says it takes under an hour, and that feels about right based on my experience.

According to recent reports, I’ve had this printer for a few months now, and I’m very pleased with it. Since I use the photos primarily with my journal, I also really appreciate how thin the photo sheets are, so they don’t bulk up the pages too much. I truly enjoy printing out my little creations, cutting out my collages and then decorating my journal with them.

I might not have my childhood back nor my Nirvana cassettes, but at least I’ve finally recaptured the joys of journaling — even if it did require a bit of help from a pocket printer.

I'm Raising My Fair Value Estimate for Berkshire Hathaway Stock. Here's What I Think It's Worth.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›.
  • I looked again at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%)(BRKB -0.36%) on Nov.
  • In a recent development, my estimate climbed mainly because of how CEO Greg Abel is managing Berkshire's money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:23AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›.

I looked again at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%)(BRKB -0.36%) on Nov. 17, and I ended up with a higher estimate of what the stock is worth. I now think the Class B shares are worth around $700 each, or about 22% over the stock's price near $575 as I write.

In a recent development, my estimate climbed mainly because of how CEO Greg Abel is managing Berkshire's money. He's been patient with the firm's huge cash pile, while the businesses Berkshire owns outright keep growing.

The $700 comes from adding up four parts: the cash and Treasury bills, the stock portfolio, the operating businesses and the insurance operation. But they don't carry equal weight.

It has been revealed that berkshire's balance sheet does a lot of the work before any business is valued. As of Sept. 30, its insurance and other businesses had around $352 billion in cash, cash equivalents and Treasury bills (net of Treasury purchases that settled in October). Its stock portfolio was worth about $336 billion more. Spread over the outstanding shares on that date, that's around $166 a Class B share in cash and about $158 in stocks. Together, they cover more than half of today's stock price.

According to recent reports, I'm counting both at full value, which is a bit generous. Berkshire would owe taxes on its $227 billion in unrealized gains if it sold, and the parent had around $20 billion in debt. Sure, taxes are due only when Berkshire sells, and it has owned some of its largest holdings for decades.

And Abel doesn't look to be in a rush to sell. Berkshire's stake in Apple has stayed at around 228 million shares for three quarters running, according to its 13F filings. Berkshire last trimmed it in the fourth quarter of 2025, Warren Buffett's final quarter as CEO.

That leaves around $377 of my estimate for the rest.

It has been revealed that in the past four quarters, BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and the manufacturing, service and retailing group earned about $25.4 billion after tax. And insurance underwriting added around $6.4 billion. Altogether, these operations earned around $31.8 billion.

According to recent reports, at $700 a share, I'm valuing them at around $800 billion, or about 25 times their total earnings. That's about the same price-to-earnings ratio the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) carries today, based on the last year of earnings.

At today's price, the market's valuing Berkshire's operations at just around 17 times earnings.

Industry observers note that put another way, the businesses are the swing factor. Almost all the gap between $575 and $700 depends on how much credit the operating companies get.

First, Berkshire's operating businesses are growing. Showing the momentum outside insurance, after-tax earnings at BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and the manufacturing, service and retailing group rose around 13% year over year through September. The OxyChem chemicals business Berkshire bought in January helped.

And BNSF's pre-tax earnings climbed around 15% in that time, with growth picking up to about 19% in the third quarter.

According to recent reports, insurance is the bumpier part. Third-quarter underwriting profit dropped around 43% year over year, driven by higher claims costs at GEICO. That sort of swing is normal for an insurer, and Berkshire itself warns that its underwriting results can be volatile from period to period.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger prize might be the float (premiums Berkshire keeps before paying claims), which stood at about $178.5 billion at the end of the third quarter. Through September, its average cost was negative, so Berkshire was effectively paid to keep it.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

In a recent development, abel's patience demonstrates in Berkshire's trading, too. In the third quarter, the S&P 500 gained around 2%, and Berkshire sold a little more stock than it bought. Meanwhile, it spent about $9.6 billion on buybacks at average prices around $500 a Class B share -- two-thirds of its $14.4 billion nine-month total.

This restraint is also why I see Berkshire as a hedge against the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Yes, Alphabet is one of its five biggest stock holdings. But most of what a buyer gets is cash, insurance, a railroad, utilities and factories, which might hold up better if AI spending ever slows.

In the end, I think around $700 is a fair value for a company whose cash and stocks alone cover more than half of today's price. The market is paying about 17 times earnings for the businesses, and I think they deserve more credit than that.

With the stock near $575, I'd be comfortable buying shares now and holding them for years. Berkshire is still my best stock pick for the next 10 years.

#62426. Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2208 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.
  • In a recent development, microsoft Outlook?
  • Something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

In a recent development, microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some problems. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

Something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these issues, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One massive reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

Sources indicate that if it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a major or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

It has been revealed that even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Sources indicate that another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

When I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he noted, “it’s bad.”.

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said.

Sources indicate that things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning last week.

In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers states CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said.

It has been revealed that despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” remarked Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

According to recent reports, the good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

It still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”.

And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella stated this week at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”.

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this major backlog of security complications in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” remarked Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

According to recent reports, it goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of concerns is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with vital, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to revision so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

Recent findings suggest that and patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s concerns on Tuesday.

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing problem.

Industry observers note that in the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

Substantial Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” mentioned Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy states.

Recent findings suggest that that means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into new software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

Industry observers note that “I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”.

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more notable than ever.

In a recent development, “You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers mentioned. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”.

Industry observers note that but consumers aren’t without power, especially when it comes to data breaches. If a company isn’t properly maintaining its systems and protecting your privacy or security online, don’t use it. Having your data hacked and compromised has become ordinary. We get letters in the mail saying someone stole data from our bank or doctor’s office, and if we jump through the following hoops, we can get 12 months of identity protection.

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

#62425. Latest Update: Microsoft claims its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Microsoft claims its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the tech giant introduced two upcoming frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks.
  • Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model demonstrates 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.
  • Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the tech giant introduced two upcoming frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model demonstrates 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft states MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

It has been revealed that this doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

According to recent reports, it’s also key to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

It has been revealed that throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these fresh models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex.

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the firm paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

Recent findings suggest that if you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As people adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the manufacturer itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Recent findings suggest that let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a tech giant is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these upcoming models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first.

A manufacturer with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

Industry observers note that A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

Industry observers note that there’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

According to recent reports, benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open glitch.

The organization also described clearly that these fresh models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

#62423. One Month and a Half-Million-Plus Folds Later, Our Machine Is Still Testing the iPhone Duo

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1110 w)

One Month and a Half-Million-Plus Folds Later, Our Machine Is Still Testing the iPhone Duo

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago.
  • How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo?
  • I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago. Every day since then, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, a dedicated machine inside CNET’s lab has been folding and unfolding it over and over again. For science.

How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of Friday, Nov. 20, we’re up to more than 565,000 folds and the Duo hasn’t broken yet. The hinge has shown signs of potential failure, however. Our technicians, as well as the cameras and sensors that are part of our testing rig, continue to monitor the situation and collect data.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built this proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close, over and over, for the past few weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Industry observers note that CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review as well as her one-month-later follow-up. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Recent findings suggest that join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a newly introduced-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Industry observers note that most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.).

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

According to recent reports, we determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Sources indicate that an industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

It has been revealed that we also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

Recent findings suggest that there’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

According to recent reports, apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • But does that expense result in real business value?
  • Also: Microsoft indicates its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
  • Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft indicates its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s massive bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

In a recent development, instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

In a recent development, then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new.

According to recent reports, what comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically notes, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your firm needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

According to recent reports, I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the organization’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the manufacturer’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

In a recent development, this means the tech giant doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

Google Gemini Partners With Watch Duty to Clear Static From Firefighter Radio
